stories.persona_identity: Amina is a 12-year-old girl and middle-school student who recently resettled as a refugee; she is vulnerable to discrimination tied to her status. Her tech comfort is low because she uses a hand-me-down phone and relies on trial-and-error rather than understanding app settings.
stories.story: After school in Harborview, Amina got a phone alert about a nearby traffic dispute and opened the community safety app to see what was happening. She posted a quick message saying she was right across from the refugee welcome center so neighbors could avoid the area. Later, wanting to be helpful, she started her own short broadcast showing the street outside the shelter. By the evening, boys from her school and a hostile neighbor had found her post and broadcast, recognized her voice and location, and shared it in a local group. Frightened, she tried to remove the video but backed out of the process and it remained visible.
stories.information_leaked: Amina’s proximity to the Harbor View Welcome Center at 214 Harbor Ave (exact street shown on the live stream banner), her username (“AminaS12”) and profile avatar, her voice and face during the broadcast, the timestamped time she was present outside the shelter after school, and her self-disclosed location in chat indicating she was across from the refugee center.

step_causing_harm: Step 2: Tap the video to watch the stream — the stream prominently displays the exact street name and Amina’s proximity (e.g., “0.1 mi · Harbor Ave”), normalizing highly granular location context for a minor.
design_problems: Proximity-first framing nudges disclosure of being ‘nearby’ without any youth-specific privacy guidance.
No contextual warning that viewing or interacting around sensitive locations (e.g., refugee centers) can create risks.

step_causing_harm: Step 5: Type and submit your comment — Amina writes that she is “across from Harbor View Welcome Center,” revealing real-time location.
Step 6: Your comment is posted and shown in chat — comment is public, persistent, and appears on the reporter’s screen where it can be screen-recorded and reshared.
design_problems: Default public comments with no location-safety prompt or child-sensitive warning before posting.
Generic ‘be respectful’ guidelines omit ‘don’t share your location’ and provide no easy ‘anonymous mode’ for minors.
Chat is designed for immediacy, encouraging impulsive disclosure in stressful situations.

step_causing_harm: Step 7: Wait for 3 seconds to start broadcast — the live broadcast publishes with the user’s precise location and time, exposing Amina’s presence outside the shelter.
Step 9: Return to the video to continue watching — viewer activity and reactions implicitly amplify and spread the stream to nearby users.
design_problems: Auto-location labeling on live broadcasts with no option to blur/obfuscate location or limit audience to trusted contacts.
No age gating, guardian approval, or safer default for minors; live is public-by-default and push-notified to nearby users.
No in-stream safety coaching to avoid filming identifiable landmarks (e.g., the shelter sign) or faces.

step_causing_harm: Step 4: Tap 'Delete Video' — destructive action is hard to understand for a novice child user without preview of consequences or alternatives (e.g., private archive).
Step 5: Tap 'Cancel' — Amina backs out and the broadcast remains available, continuing exposure.
design_problems: Confusing confirmation language and visual hierarchy; easy to abandon deletion unintentionally.
No explanation that previously shared links, notifications, or caches will persist even if deletion succeeds.
No simpler ‘Hide everywhere now’ option or one-tap privacy lock for minors.

stories.leakage_source: NeighborNet’s public chat and auto-labeled Live+ broadcasts (design choices that publish precise location and persistent comments), compounded by other users who screen-recorded and reshared Amina’s content.
stories.leak_to: Nearby NeighborNet users receiving the live push and browsing the feed, classmates who follow the neighborhood area, and a local anti-immigrant Telegram/Facebook group where the clip was reposted.

harms.harm: Physical harms (stalking or targeting near the shelter)
harms.cause: Live+ and comments publicly exposed Amina’s real-time presence and precise location outside the refugee center.
The app’s public-by-default design made it easy to identify her as connected to the refugee center and redistribute that evidence.
Public comments and the broadcast were linked to her username and voice, enabling peers to mock and stigmatize her.
Persistent visibility of the post and re-shares created ongoing anxiety and fear of being watched.

harms.harm: Autonomy harms (lack of control, thwarted expectations, chilling effects)
harms.cause: Confusing deletion flow and continued availability of reshared content undermined her ability to retract the post, discouraging future participation in community spaces.
Exposure led to tension at school and within the local community, damaging trust and support networks.

stories.consequences: Amina is mocked at school and confronted by a hostile neighbor near the shelter. Her family restricts her movements, and she withdraws from local programs and the app, missing out on language support and neighborhood safety updates. She experiences ongoing anxiety when leaving the shelter or using community apps.

stories.persona_identity: Eleanor is a 72-year-old retired school librarian living alone; as an elderly woman experiencing mild cognitive decline, she relies on a caregiver for device settings. Her low tech comfort comes from memory lapses and anxiety with fast, multi-step prompts on newer apps.
stories.story: During a quiet afternoon in Riverview, Eleanor opened a neighborhood safety app to report what she thought was a gas smell in her building. Midway through, she tried to back out but accidentally stayed on air. The stream briefly showed her living room, revealing her exact location and personal items on the table. The app automatically sent the video to nearby users, who reacted and shared it. Later, her caregiver helped her delete the clip from her history, but neighbors had already seen and saved it, and the link kept circulating in local group chats.
stories.information_leaked: Precise home location and unit-level proximity; interior of her residence; visible prescription pill organizer labeled with medication names; mobility cane; mail showing bank brand and partial address; her voice indicating she is home alone; timestamped evidence of her routine.

step_causing_harm: Step 6: Tap 'Stay Live'. Eleanor intends to cancel but selects the option that keeps the broadcast going.
Step 7: System action confirms nearby related incidents and surfaces the stream to neighbors, increasing exposure.
design_problems: Confusing end/cancel flow with a prominent 'Stay Live' option that is easier to tap than 'End', creating error-prone decisions for low-comfort users.
No protective pause or private preview; the app defaults to public broadcasting with location attached once eligibility is met.
Automatic surfacing to nearby users without a clear, plain-language consent checkpoint tailored for vulnerable users.

step_causing_harm: Step 5: Tap 'Delete'. Eleanor believes deletion removes the video everywhere, but it only disappears from her list while copies and shares persist.
design_problems: Deletion language implies finality without disclosing that prior shares, downloads, or cached links remain accessible to others.
No retroactive recall of push notifications or purge from content delivery caches; no notice to recipients who saved or downloaded the clip.
The platform allows others to download or share broadcasts, yet the delete action does not revoke or flag those copies.

stories.leakage_source: The community safety app’s auto-broadcast with precise location and its distribution features (nearby surfacing, notifications, and permissive sharing/downloading).
stories.leak_to: Nearby app users within the notification radius; neighbors who received push alerts; recipients in local group chats where the stream link or saved copy was shared.

harms.cause: The app auto-exposed her home interior and health cues to neighbors, leading to public comments and ongoing circulation despite her attempt to delete.
Viewers inferred frailty and diminished independence from visible medications and mobility aids, altering neighbors’ perceptions.

harms.harm: Autonomy Harms — Lack of Control and Thwarted Expectations
harms.cause: Confusing live-ending flow and deletion that didn’t remove shared copies undermined her ability to control what was posted and who could see it.
Revealing that she was home alone with medications and her exact location increased risks of targeting by opportunistic actors.
Bank-branded mail in the frame enabled targeted phishing and fraud attempts by local viewers who recognized the institution.
Her caregiver increased monitoring and restricted app access after the incident, straining trust and reducing Eleanor’s autonomy.

stories.consequences: Eleanor becomes anxious and stops using the app for genuine emergencies; neighbors gossip about her health; she receives suspicious calls referencing her bank; her caregiver locks down her phone permissions, leading to further loss of independence and increased isolation.

stories.persona_identity: Jamal is a 15-year-old boy and high school student; as a minor using social apps he’s vulnerable to adult surveillance and misinterpretation, and he’s highly tech-comfortable because he routinely manages alt accounts and tight privacy settings to avoid location tagging.
stories.story: After school on a Tuesday, Jamal starts a quick live alert about an ambulance stop outside Roosevelt High so his friends know to avoid the bus stop. He assumes it will be seen mostly by peers and won’t pinpoint him. Within minutes, the live is pushed across the neighborhood, tagged to the exact street near the school. Later, Jamal notices his own stream prominently featured in the feed and replies in chat to calm rumors using his main profile, which makes it easy for adults nearby to recognize him and link him to the scene.
stories.information_leaked: Precise real-time location near 1150 Pine St by Roosevelt High; timestamp of presence; association with a school-related incident; Jamal’s primary display name shown in chat; evidence of his viewing and commenting activity tied to the incident within the neighborhood feed.

step_causing_harm: Step 5: Wait for 3 seconds to start broadcast — the live goes out showing 'LIVE' with the user’s location next to the incident type.
Step 6: System action decides related incidents are nearby (answer: yes) — the platform distributes the broadcast to neighbors within range.
design_problems: Location is displayed precisely on live by default with no teen-specific or granular location controls.
Automatic neighborhood notifications/amplification when an incident is detected within 0.25 miles, without clear opt-in or audience scoping for minors.

step_causing_harm: Step 2: System surfaces live streams in the News feed with animated thumbnails and a 'LIVE' tag, making the broadcast broadly discoverable beyond Jamal’s intended peer audience.
design_problems: Public-by-default distribution in a neighborhood-wide feed; no easy way to restrict discovery to a trusted list or teen-only audience.
Algorithmic surfacing tied to place increases identifiability and context collapse (peers, parents, school staff all see it).

step_causing_harm: Step 5: Type and submit your comment — Jamal replies from his main profile, revealing his recognizable display name and mentioning the school.
Step 6: Your comment is posted and shown in chat — the identity cue and school reference persist publicly with the video.
design_problems: No clear 'posting as' indicator or easy account switcher within Live chat; defaults to primary profile.
Civility notice appears, but there’s no privacy warning that comments are public and persist or that they can expose identity and place.

stories.leakage_source: Default app behaviors (precise location tagging and neighborhood-wide notifications/surfacing) combined with Jamal’s public comment from his main profile.
stories.leak_to: Nearby adults and teens using NeighborNet (neighbors, school staff monitoring the area, and a family friend in the neighborhood group), plus anyone who watches the replay in the following 24 hours.

harms.cause: The live ties Jamal to a school-related emergency scene, leading adults to infer involvement because the app prominently tags location and time.
Unexpected adult scrutiny and messages after the live is algorithmically surfaced beyond his peer circle.

harms.harm: Autonomy harm (thwarted expectations and lack of control)
harms.cause: Public-by-default location tagging and distribution without a clear audience selector or teen protections undermines Jamal’s intention to alert only peers.
Adults in his network (including a family friend) see the live and his comment, triggering parental conflict and mistrust.
Being visibly associated with recording a school-side incident may mark him as a 'snitch' to older students who saw the public live.

stories.consequences: A school resource officer questions Jamal the next day; his parent restricts his phone use; peers accuse him of snitching; he stops using the app and increases the mental load of managing multiple identities to avoid future exposure.

stories.persona_identity: Liam is a 35-year-old man working as a community pharmacist; he manages Crohn’s disease (a chronic illness) and is moderately tech-comfortable because he uses mobile apps daily at work but avoids advanced settings and deep configuration.
stories.story: During a burst water-main incident on Maple Avenue, Liam opened the community safety app to see what was happening and then decided to go live from his apartment stoop to warn delivery drivers about the blocked street. The app labeled his broadcast with his nearby cross-street and pushed it to neighbors. In his hurried stream, a biologic injection box and sharps container were visible in the background. Afterward, feeling uneasy, he hid the video from his profile, but neighbors had already received a notification preview and some kept seeing it in their feed. Later that evening, he commented on another live update mentioning he’d had an infusion and was immunosuppressed, hoping people would avoid creating dust near his building. The app’s defaults and public chat tied these details to his name and neighborhood.
stories.information_leaked: Liam’s approximate home block (near 410 Maple Ave), time-stamped presence at home during the incident, visible evidence of Crohn’s treatment (biologic injection box, sharps container) in his live stream, and explicit disclosure of recent infusion/immunosuppression in a public comment linked to his profile.

step_causing_harm: Step 4: Tap the video to watch the stream — upon joining, Liam’s account presence becomes visible to the live host and nearby viewers.
design_problems: Auto-discloses viewer presence/identity without a privacy or 'anonymous viewing' mode.
No clear pre-join notice that joining a live can reveal identity to others.

step_causing_harm: Step 7: Active live broadcast begins and is labeled with Liam’s nearby location; his camera view inadvertently includes medication packaging and a sharps container.
design_problems: Precise-or-near-precise location labeling is enabled by default on broadcasts.
No pre-broadcast safety check (e.g., background blur or privacy scan) to warn about sensitive items in frame.
No easy toggle to hide or obfuscate location while still allowing the broadcast.
Push notifications amplify exposure by sending labeled thumbnails to nearby users.

step_causing_harm: Step 4: Tap 'Hide Video From Profile' — Liam assumes the content is fully withdrawn from public view, but previews and notifications persist in others’ feeds.
design_problems: Scope of 'Hide' is unclear and does not revoke push notification previews or cached feed entries.
UI copy promises immediate removal from public view but does not disclose caching/notification limitations.
No option to purge thumbnails or revoke shares after hiding.

step_causing_harm: Step 8: Comment is posted publicly and tied to Liam’s profile within a location-specific live chat.
design_problems: Comments default to public and are profile-linked without audience controls.
No in-context health privacy warning or suggestion to use pseudonyms for sensitive disclosures.
Location and time context in the live chat increases identifiability.

stories.leakage_source: NeighborNet app defaults (auto-location labeling, public viewer presence, public comments) and its push-notification previews.
stories.leak_to: Nearby NeighborNet subscribers within the incident radius, the live host and viewers, and anyone who received or later viewed the push-notification preview in their feed.

harms.cause: The live stream’s labeled location and visible medical supplies, plus the public comment about an infusion, associate Liam’s identity with a chronic illness in his local community.
Persistent previews and neighbors recognizing his treatment details despite hiding the video create anxiety and loss of peace of mind.

harms.harm: Autonomy harms — Lack of control and Thwarted expectations
harms.cause: The ‘Hide’ function does not remove thumbnails or revoke prior notifications, and the app offers no clear controls to broadcast without showing location or to post comments privately.
Publicly tying his home block with visible medications may increase risk of targeted theft or harassment.
Local acquaintances or clients who view the content may infer health-related limitations, potentially affecting work opportunities or trust in his reliability.

stories.consequences: A neighbor messages Liam about ‘seeing his injections,’ and screenshots of the notification preview circulate in a neighborhood group. Liam feels exposed, stops using the app for safety updates, and avoids future broadcasts. He worries about being judged at work and secures his apartment more aggressively, incurring extra costs and stress.

stories.persona_identity: Arjun is a 28-year-old man who works as an administrative assistant at a neighborhood nonprofit; he uses a powered wheelchair due to a mobility impairment, which places him in the “person with physical disability” vulnerability group. His tech comfort is medium because he uses mobile apps daily for scheduling and transit but tends to avoid deeper privacy settings or advanced configurations.
stories.story: On his way home from physical therapy, Arjun used the community safety app to report a car blocking the curb ramp outside 219 Maple Ave in Oakland at around 7:45 p.m. The live video clearly showed his powered wheelchair and the entrance area of his apartment building. The app sent a nearby alert with the street and distance to local users, and a neighbor recognized his building from the stream and commented about the resident in the wheelchair. That night, Arjun searched the app and found the recording publicly indexed to his block. Worried, he hid the video from his profile, but the alert preview and shares had already circulated among neighbors.
stories.information_leaked: Assistive device usage (powered wheelchair) visible in the video; approximate home location and entrance context (219 Maple Ave, Oakland); routine timing (post-therapy commute around 7:45 p.m.); username and face; precise neighborhood geotag and distance metadata delivered to nearby users; viewer metrics indicating distribution scope.

step_causing_harm: Step 6: Tap 'Stay Live' — the broadcast becomes publicly viewable with location labeling while showing Arjun and his powered wheelchair.
Step 8: Viewer chat and reactions appear during the live session — neighbors can identify contextual details (building entrance, mailbox cluster) and speculate about Arjun’s disability and residence.
design_problems: Default public broadcast with precise location labeling exposes the streamer’s disability and near-home setting without granular privacy warnings.
No pre-broadcast privacy guardrails (e.g., blur assistive devices/faces, suppress exact location, limit audience) or disability-aware prompts.
Real-time chat amplifies identification and speculation without default moderation or protective filters for sensitive attributes.

step_causing_harm: Step 2: Tap a recorded stream thumbnail to view details — the recording is indexed to a specific block and displays location context and preview imagery that includes Arjun’s wheelchair.
Step 3: Tap the video to watch the stream — replay availability extends exposure of disability status and near-home location beyond the live window.
design_problems: Map indexing of streams to specific blocks by default, with preview frames showing assistive devices, increases identifiability.
Replay persists for a period without clear, user-facing controls to suppress precise location or sensitive visual details.
Viewer metrics and distribution indicators normalize broad dissemination of potentially sensitive content.

step_causing_harm: Step 4: Tap 'Hide Video From Profile' — offers a sense of immediate privacy, but previously delivered alerts and shares remain outside the user’s control, leading to a feeling of powerlessness.
design_problems: Ambiguous scope of 'Hide' (profile-focused) fails to revoke or purge previously pushed alerts, cached thumbnails, or shared links.
No clear option to remove location indexing or purge CDNs/preview images across the ecosystem, nor guidance on residual distribution.
Insufficient disclosure that hiding does not retroactively undo distribution, creating a failure-to-inform scenario.

stories.leakage_source: The community safety app’s default public live broadcast with precise location labeling, automatic map/news indexing, and replay availability; compounded by neighbors who rewatch or share the alert.
stories.leak_to: Nearby app users within the alert radius (including neighbors and the building manager who uses the app), and anyone who receives shared links or screenshots.

harms.harm: Psychological Harms — Emotional distress and disturbance
harms.cause: The app pushes a geolabeled broadcast and retains a replay that visibly reveals Arjun’s disability and near-home environment, triggering anxiety about being recognized and watched.

harms.harm: Autonomy Harms — Lack of Control and Failure to Inform
harms.cause: Defaults to public indexing and chat without clear, disability-aware privacy warnings or granular controls; the 'Hide' action does not explain that alerts and shares persist, undermining user control.

harms.harm: Discrimination Harms — Heightened risk of bias or surveillance
harms.cause: Exposure of assistive device usage and home proximity may prompt neighbors or property management to scrutinize, stereotype, or monitor Arjun.

stories.consequences: A neighbor publicly identifies Arjun as the wheelchair user in his building; the building manager questions him about streaming on the premises; Arjun feels watched and avoids using the app and going out at the same time, leading to anxiety, reduced participation in local activities, and a chilling effect on reporting accessibility issues.

stories.persona_identity: Maya, 30, is a gender non-conforming community outreach coordinator at an LGBTQ+ youth center; her visibility makes her vulnerable to targeting, and her high tech comfort comes from years of privacy‑conscious, power‑user habits managing digital tools for advocacy.
stories.story: On a Friday evening in Astoria, Queens, Maya opened her community safety app to check on a nearby disturbance reported outside the LGBTQ+ youth center where she volunteers. She tapped into a live neighborhood stream and posted a brief warning in the chat asking the host not to film the youth as they exited. The host read her handle and paraphrased her message on-air, repeating the center’s corner. The stream ended and was later available as a recording with the chat and captions attached. Over the weekend, people in a hostile neighborhood Facebook group circulated the clip, linking her handle to a reused pseudonym on a dating profile, identifying her as a volunteer at the center.
stories.information_leaked: Persistent association between Maya’s pseudonymous app handle (e.g., "MxRiverNYC"), the LGBTQ+ youth center location (12th St & Greeley Ave, Astoria), her volunteer affiliation, exact time of presence during the incident, and a cross-link to her dating profile where she uses the same or similar handle.

step_causing_harm: Step 3: News card expands to a detail page with location and map — any subsequent comments are contextually tied to a precise place and timestamp on an incident page that remains browsable.
Step 4: Tap the video to watch the stream — the session and its discussion are retained with the recording, creating a durable link between viewer comments and the incident location.
design_problems: Step 3: The app prominently exposes granular location and time on a publicly accessible incident page without offering a privacy mode for sensitive venues.
Step 4: Comments and metadata persist with replays by default; no ephemeral mode or ability to prevent chat from being archived and searchable with the video.

step_causing_harm: Step 6: Your comment is posted and shown in chat — the handle and message are published publicly and retained with the incident.
Step 7: Return to the video to continue watching — the host reads the comment aloud, and the platform’s captions/transcripts further index the handle and location in the replay.
design_problems: Step 6: Public-by-default comments with persistent storage; no warning that sensitive identity/location details will be permanently attached to a public incident record.
Step 7: Auto-captioning/transcription makes the handle and location searchable; no control to mask handles in replays or to redact sensitive place names mentioned on-air.

stories.leakage_source: NeighborNet’s default public archiving of Live+ chat and auto-captioned replays that index usernames and location context with no ephemeral or redaction controls.
stories.leak_to: Local viewers, hostile neighborhood social media groups that circulate the replay, acquaintances and coworkers who browse the app, and anyone searching the incident by location or keywords.

harms.cause: The app permanently attaches her handle and a volunteer affiliation to a sensitive location, enabling cross-platform doxxing and stigma.
Persistent replay and circulation of the clip amplify harassment anxiety and fear of being targeted when returning to the center.

harms.harm: Autonomy harms — lack of control and chilling effects
harms.cause: No option to post ephemerally or redact comments from replays deters her from participating in local safety discussions.
Indexing her handle with an LGBTQ+ venue exposes her to anti-LGBTQ harassment and potential bias from neighbors or employers.
Coworkers and neighbors discover her volunteer role and identity through the replay, straining personal and professional relationships.

stories.consequences: Maya receives harassing messages referencing the youth center; she locks down and deletes several profiles, avoids walking to the center at normal hours, and stops commenting on neighborhood safety updates. The stress affects her work and community involvement, and she limits her participation in local mutual-aid efforts due to fear of renewed exposure.
